newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl warns coalition against new attacks on Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Kohl warns coalition against new attacks on Waigel.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, back from a Far East trip, demanded on Monday an end to budget squabbling in his fractious centre-right coalition government.
Kohl said his Christian Democratic Party (CDU) wanted to retain the coalition and warned junior partners, the Free Democrats (FDP) to halt attacks on Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

A shortfall of several billion marks (dollars) for the 1997 budget has opened up deep rifts between the CDU/CSU and the shaky FDP, which sees the crisis as a threat to a tax-cutting image vital to its political survival.

Backing the embattled finance minister, Kohl returned to work in Bonn after an eight-day Asia trip and told the FDP that it would fail in efforts to raise its public profile at the expense of the coalition.
Kohl said the centre-right coalition would hold together because there was no viable alternative.
"We want this coalition and we want it to continue," he said after meeting Christian Democratic Party (CDU) leaders.
But he warned the FDP it would be making a mistake if it thought it could raise its own standing among voters at the expense of the CDU and its Bavarian sister party the CSU.

"Anyone in any of the coalition parties who believes they can raise their profile at the cost of the others is mistaken," Kohl said. "The coalition is successful as a whole and everyone has their share in it."

The CDU/CSU, caught between a pledge to meet the European Union's Maastricht budget criteria and fear of a backlash against radical state spending cuts, wants to keep its budget options open and suspects the FDP wants to play tax-cutter at its expense.

The row smouldered while Kohl was on a three-nation Asian tour last week. The FDP accused Waigel of presenting misleading figures on the 1997 deficit and threatened to leave the coalition if he tried to finance the gap with tax increases.
"Theo Waigel deserves all our support, especially in this difficult time," Kohl said. "I say that quite clearly as chancellor and chairman of the CDU."

Kohl said political divisions in Germany were clear cut, with conservatives and centrists who back the coalition facing off against the left-leaning spectrum behind the Social Democrats (SPD), Greens and reform communist PDS.
Kohl appeared to be hinting that the FDP had nowhere else to turn.

That view was underscored by an Emnid research institute opinion poll published on Monday. It showed the ruling coalition with 43 percent compared to 44 percent for the SPD and Greens together. The Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS) had six percent.
Despite Kohl's appeal, the debate over financing could heat up again this week.

Federal and state tax experts are due to meet later in the week. Der Spiegel news magazine said they are likely to report that 1997 tax revenue will be nine to 11 billion marks ($7.25 billion) short of expectations because of slow growth and high unemployment.
Waigel is already struggling to find between three and four billion marks to cover a known budget gap for 1997.
The finance minister, who must present a balanced budget to the relevant parliamentary committee on November 14, said the figures would be presented at the end of the week.
"We will wait for the tax estimates," he said.
All ministries will have to make cuts in order to achieve a balanced budget for 1997, he said, but added the defence budget would not be hit as hard as in the past.
